newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- NOV 15.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- NOV 15.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek general press:

--The Greek Parliament in a moment of crisis. Yesterday's passage of the government's bill on settling debts to the state could have been voted down if the absent MPs from ruling party PASOK and main opposition New Democracy had been at the session. A number of PASOK MPs voted against the bill, which was eventually passed but the question of whether both the ruling party and the opposition are in a position to do their jobs remains.

--A new opinion poll shows that the barrage of criticism New Democracy leader Miltiades Evert has had to fend off was the major reason for the party's defeat in the September 22 elections. Some 41.5 percent said that PASOK's election campaign was better and 35 percent that the economic policies promoted by PASOK leader (and now Prime Minister) Costas Simitis were more attractive to New Democracy voters.

--The General Confederation of Workers of Greece (GSEE) has called for a 'workers' risk' charge to be imposed on social security contributions, following the release of a GSEE report on accidents in the workplace. The report says there are 120 workplace-related deaths per year and 25,000 injuries: the cost to the Social Security Foundation is estimated to be 25 billion drachmas.

--Prime Minister Costas Simitis lashes out at possible mutineers at the ruling party's executive bureau meeting last night. "If we fall, we all fall together," Simitis warns dissenters worried about the fall-out from the coming austere budget and economic measures.

--Wednesday night's bomb attack at the Athens Polytechnic School will not derail traditional celebrations marking the anniversary of the 1973 student uprising. Proposals to shut down the school's premises for the duration are rejected and the National Union of Students and Polytechnic board had said they will assume all responsibility. Fourteen thousand police officers are on standby. TA NEA

--The Supreme Court is investigating the case of a drug trafficker allowed to walk after serving only one year of his 16-year sentence. Inconsistency in the sentencing of drug-related crimes appears to be prevalent as a drug user found with 1.7 grams of heroin gets four years jail and an Albanian with five kilos fails to show up for his trial after the Supreme Court releases him from preliminary detention.

--One pleasant surprise amidst the unpleasant economic measures to be announced on Tuesday: the government breaks the 'tradition' of an annual increase in duties on cigarettes and alcohol. Other measures: public servants to get 8.5 percent increases through the new wage scale, the last tax-free bonds go on sale next week before they are hit with 7.5 percent, the tax scale will not change to prevent revenue losses, and increased duties for vehicles, yachts and planes.

--Shopkeepers on downtown Patission street fear a rerun of the free-for-all riots by self-styled anarchists and hoodlums during last year's Polytechnic anniversary. "They'll trash our stores for the 16th time," shopkeepers say as they take their own measures to protect their property.

--The developments at the Athens Stock exchange, and the disappointing performance of the bourse on the first full day of trading yesterday after a three-day closure, prompts New Democracy to call for a parliamentary investigatory committee into the crisis. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
